{{Short description|Static exact solution in general relativity}}
{{General relativity sidebar|solutions}}
In [[Albert Einstein|Einstein]]'s theory of [[general relativity]], the '''interior Schwarzschild metric''' (also '''interior Schwarzschild solution''' or '''Schwarzschild fluid solution''') is an [[Exact solutions in general relativity|exact solution]] for the [[gravitational field]] in the interior of a non-rotating spherical body which consists of an [[incompressible fluid]] (implying that [[density]] is constant throughout the body) and has zero [[pressure]] at the surface. This is a static solution, meaning that it does not change over time. It was discovered by [[Karl Schwarzschild]] in 1916, who earlier had found the [[exterior Schwarzschild metric]].<ref name="Schwarzschild_ext">{{cite journal|author=Karl Schwarzschild|title=Über das Gravitationsfeld eines Massenpunktes nach der Einsteinschen Theorie|trans-title=On the gravitational field of a point mass following Einstein's theory|url=https://de.wikisource.org/wiki/%C3%9Cber_das_Gravitationsfeld_eines_Massenpunktes_nach_der_Einsteinschen_Theorie|journal=Sitzungsberichte der Königlich-Preussischen Akademie der Wissenschaften|location=Berlin|year=1916|language=de|pages=189–196|bibcode=1916SPAW.......189S }}</ref>

==Mathematics==
[[File:3D Spherical.svg|thumb|Spherical coordinates]]
The interior Schwarzschild metric is framed in a [[spherical coordinate system]] with the body's centre located at the origin, plus the time coordinate. Its [[line element]] is<ref name="Schwarzschild">{{cite journal|author=Karl Schwarzschild|title=Über das Gravitationsfeld einer Kugel aus inkompressibler Flüssigkeit nach der Einsteinschen Theorie|trans-title=On the gravitational field of a ball of incompressible fluid following Einstein's theory|url=https://de.wikisource.org/wiki/Gravitationsfeld_einer_Kugel_aus_inkompressibler_Fl%C3%BCssigkeit|journal=Sitzungsberichte der Königlich-Preussischen Akademie der Wissenschaften|location=Berlin|year=1916|language=de|pages=424–434|bibcode=1916skpa.conf..424S }}</ref><ref name="Flb2003">{{cite book|author=Torsten Fließbach|title=Allgemeine Relativitätstheorie|trans-title=General Theory of Relativity|edition=4th|language=de|publisher=Spektrum Akademischer Verlag|year=2003|pages=231–241|isbn=3-8274-1356-7}}</ref>
: <math>\begin{align}
 c^2\, d\tau^2 =&
  -\frac{1}{4} \left(3 \sqrt{1 - \frac{r_s}{r_g}} - \sqrt{1 - \frac{r^2 r_s}{r_g^3}}\right)^2 c^2 \,dt^2 \\
 &{} + \left(1 - \frac{r^2 r_s}{r_g^3}\right)^{-1} \,dr^2 + r^2 (d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta \,d\varphi^2),
\end{align}</math>
where
: <math>\tau</math> is the [[proper time]] (time measured by a clock moving along the same [[world line]] with the [[test particle]]),
: <math>c</math> is the [[speed of light]],
: <math>t</math> is the time coordinate (measured by a stationary clock located infinitely far from the spherical body),
: <math>r</math> is the Schwarzschild radial coordinate; each surface of constant <math>t</math> and <math>r</math> has the geometry of a sphere with measurable (proper) circumference <math>2\pi r</math> and area <math>4\pi r^2</math> (as by the usual formulas), but the warping of space means that the proper distance from each shell to the center of the body is greater than <math>r</math>,
: <math>\theta</math> is the [[colatitude]] (angle from north, in units of [[radian]]s),
: <math>\varphi</math> is the [[longitude]] (also in radians),
: <math>r_s</math> is the [[Schwarzschild radius]] of the body, which is related to its mass <math>M</math> by <math>r_s = 2GM/c^2</math>, where <math>G</math> is the [[gravitational constant]] (for ordinary stars and planets, this is much less than their proper radius),
: <math>r_g</math> is the value of the <math>r</math> coordinate at the body's surface; this is less than its proper (measurable interior) radius, although for the Earth the difference is only about 1.4&nbsp;millimetres.

This solution is valid for <math>r \leq r_g</math>. For a complete metric of the sphere's gravitational field, the interior Schwarzschild metric has to be matched with the exterior one,
: <math>
 -c^2 \,d\tau^2 =
  \left(1 - \frac{r_s}{r}\right) c^2 \,dt^2 - \left(1 - \frac{r_s}{r}\right)^{-1} \,dr^2
  - r^2 (d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta \,d\varphi^2),
</math>
at the surface. It can easily be seen that the two have the same value at the surface, i.e., at <math>r = r_g</math>.

===Other formulations===
Defining a parameter <math>\mathcal{R}^2 = r_g^3 / r_s</math>, we get
: <math>\begin{align}
 -c^2 d\tau^2 =& -\frac{1}{4} \left(3 \sqrt{1 - \frac {r^2_g}{\mathcal{R}^2}}
  - \sqrt{1 - \frac{r^2}{\mathcal{R}^2}}\right)^2 c^2 \,dt^2 \\
  &{} + \left(1 - \frac{r^2}{\mathcal{R}^2}\right)^{-1} \,dr^2 + r^2 (d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta \,d\varphi^2).
\end{align}</math>

We can also define an alternative radial coordinate <math>\eta = \arcsin \frac{r}{\mathcal{R}}</math> and a corresponding parameter <math>\eta_g = \arcsin \frac{r_g}{\mathcal{R}} = \arcsin \sqrt{\frac{r_s}{r_g}}</math>, yielding<ref>{{cite journal |author=R. Burghardt |title=Interior Schwarzschild Solution and Free Fall |journal=Austrian Reports on Gravitation |year=2009 |url=http://members.wavenet.at/arg/Wpdf/WIff.pdf |access-date=2016-05-05 |archive-date=2017-03-05 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170305020540/http://members.wavenet.at/arg/Wpdf/WIff.pdf |url-status=dead}}</ref>
: <math>
 c^2 d\tau^2 =
  \left(\frac{3 \cos \eta_g - \cos \eta}{2}\right)^2 c^2 \,dt^2
 - \frac{dr^2}{\cos^2 \eta} - r^2 (d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta \,d\varphi^2).
</math>

==Properties==

===Volume===
With <math>g_{rr} = (1-r_s r^2/r_g^3)^{-1}</math> and the area <math>A = 4 \pi r^2</math>, the integral for the proper volume is
: <math>V = \int_0^{r_g} A \sqrt{g_{rr}} \,dr = 2 \pi \left(\frac{r_g^{9/2} \arcsin \sqrt{\dfrac{r_s}{r_g}}}{r_s^{3/2}} - \frac{r_g^4 \sqrt{1 - \dfrac{r_s}{r_g}}}{r_s}\right),</math>
which is larger than the volume of a euclidean reference shell.

===Density===
The fluid has a constant density by definition. It is given by
:<math>\rho = \frac{M}{\frac{4\pi}{3}r_g^3} = \frac{3}{\kappa \mathcal{R}^2},</math>
where <math>\kappa = 8\pi G / c^2</math> is the [[Einstein gravitational constant]].<ref name="Flb2003" /><ref name="Florides" /> It may be counterintuitive that the density is the mass divided by the volume of a sphere with radius <math>r_g</math>, which seems to disregard that this is less than the proper radius, and that space inside the body is curved so that the volume formula for a "flat" sphere shouldn't hold at all. However, <math>M</math> is the mass measured from the outside, for example by observing a test particle orbiting the gravitating body (the "[[Johannes Kepler|Kepler]] mass"), which in general relativity is not necessarily equal to the proper mass. This mass difference exactly cancels out the difference of the volumes.

===Pressure and stability===
The pressure of the incompressible fluid can be found by calculating the [[Einstein tensor]] <math>G_{\mu\nu}</math> from the metric. The Einstein tensor is [[Diagonal matrix|diagonal]] (i.e., all off-diagonal elements are zero), meaning there are no [[shear stress]]es, and has equal values for the three spatial diagonal components, meaning pressure is [[isotropy|isotropic]]. Its value is
:<math>p=\rho c^2 \frac{\cos\eta-\cos\eta_g}{3\cos\eta_g-\cos\eta}.</math>
As expected, the pressure is zero at the surface of the sphere and increases towards the centre. It becomes infinite at the centre if <math>\cos \eta_g = 1/3</math>, which corresponds to <math>r_s = \frac{8}{9} r_g</math> or <math>\eta_g \approx 70.5^\circ</math>, which is true for a body that is extremely dense or large. Such a body suffers [[gravitational collapse]] into a [[black hole]]. As this is a time dependent process, the Schwarzschild solution does not hold any longer.<ref name="Schwarzschild" /><ref name="Flb2003" />

===Redshift===
[[Gravitational redshift]] for radiation from the sphere's surface (for example, light from a star) is
:<math>z = \frac 1 {\cos \eta_g} -1.</math>
From the stability condition <math>\cos \eta_g > 1/3</math> follows <math>z < 2</math>.<ref name="Flb2003" />

==Visualization==
[[File:Schwarzschild interior.jpg|thumb|[[Embedding]] of a Schwarzschild metric's slice in three-dimensional Euclidean space. The interior solution is the darker cap at the bottom.<br />This embedding should not be confused with the unrelated concept of a [[gravity well]].]]

The spatial [[Curvature of Riemannian manifolds|curvature]] of the interior Schwarzschild metric can be visualized by taking a slice (1) with constant time and (2) through the sphere's equator, i.e. <math>t = const., \theta = \pi/2</math>. This two-dimensional slice can be [[Embedding|embedded]] in a three-dimensional Euclidean space and then takes the shape of a [[spherical cap]] with radius <math>\mathcal{R}</math> and half opening angle <math>\eta_g</math>. Its [[Gaussian curvature]] <math>K</math> is proportional to the fluid's density and equals <math>\mathcal{R}^{-2} = r_s / r_g^3 = \rho \kappa / 3</math>. As the exterior metric can be embedded in the same way (yielding [[Flamm's paraboloid]]), a slice of the complete solution can be drawn like this:<ref name="Florides">{{cite journal|title=A New Interior Schwarzschild Solution|author=P. S. Florides|journal=Proceedings of the Royal Society of London. Series A, Mathematical and Physical Sciences|volume=337|issue=1611|year=1974|pages=529–535|jstor=78530|doi=10.1098/rspa.1974.0065|bibcode=1974RSPSA.337..529F|s2cid=122449954 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|author=R. Burghardt|title=New Embedding of Schwarzschild Geometry. II. Interior Solution|journal=Austrian Reports on Gravitation|year=2009|url=http://members.wavenet.at/arg/Wpdf/W5I.pdf|access-date=2016-05-03|archive-date=2016-05-08|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160508134520/http://members.wavenet.at/arg/Wpdf/W5I.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref>

[[File:Schwarzschild cross section.svg|frameless|center|upright=3]]

In this graphic, the blue circular arc represents the interior metric, and the black [[parabola|parabolic]] arcs with the equation <math>w = 2 \sqrt{r_s (r - r_s)}</math> represent the exterior metric, or Flamm's paraboloid. The <math>\eta</math>-coordinate is the angle measured from the centre of the cap, that is, from "above" the slice. The proper radius of the sphere – intuitively, the length of a measuring rod spanning from its centre to a point on its surface – is half the length of the circular arc, or <math>\eta_g \mathcal{R}</math>.

This is a purely geometric visualization and does not imply a physical "fourth spatial dimension" into which space would be curved. (Intrinsic curvature does not imply [[extrinsic curvature]].)

==History==
The interior Schwarzschild solution was the first [[static spherically symmetric perfect fluid]] solution that was found. It was published on 24 February 1916, only three months after [[Einstein's field equations]] and one month after Schwarzschild's exterior solution.<ref name="Schwarzschild_ext" /><ref name="Schwarzschild" />
